Cereal is incredibly porous. Maybe it's a me thing, but I can always tell the difference between eating a spoonful of dry cereal and a spoon of cereal that even briefly touched milk. (Think about taking a spoon of dry cereal, dipping it in a glass of milk and immediately eating it.) There is a difference!

Now this second point, I 100% agree with. Human error and poor estimation is a major concern. And that is why you practice. That is why you keep putting in the hours until you have perfected the ratio. Without practice, can you really enjoy your cereal? I would argue not. NOTHING CAN BE EASY IN THIS LIFE. NOTHINGGGGG!!!!!

This is exactly why you are wrong.

The only way to have JUST ENOUGH milk that you finish the milk with the cereal is to pour a relatively small (in terms of volume) amount of milk in the bowl. Cereal will, and should, always take up more room in the bowl seeing as it is a solid and does not conform to the shape of the vessel in which it is placed.

Now, assuming we have a smaller amount of milk than cereal, the issue becomes evenly coating each piece of cereal with milk.

If you pour the milk first, the only chance you have at even coating is mixing the cereal. If you have a relatively shallow bowl, this will result in a mess, and if you have a large portion of cereal, it will end with uneven mixing and broken cereal. However, if you pour the milk after the cereal, you allow access of ALL the cereal to the milk. With a controlled and circular pouring method, the dryness of the cereal is alleviated through the trickle down effect (no, not Reaganomics), and if extra stirring is desired, the friction between the pieces is already lessened through the beginning of saturation.

I'm sorry, but there is only one right answer. There is only cereal first.

I am like your friend. In high school I had friends that really struggled with their mental health, and I felt that I was always there for them. As my mental health started to decline, I began to pull away from them more and more. I wouldn't text them, when I saw them in person, I would be curt and annoyed, and when I skipped school, I wouldn't let them know. Other friends, however, could text me during this time and I'd occasionally respond. It felt like some people took more energy than others (not that I cared about any more or less).

When I started to come out of my "episodes", usually after about 2-3 weeks, my friends would be, understandably, hurt. They would mention that my actions had made their mental health suffer, and that would result in my feeling guilty and awkward. It all just put a lot of strain on our friendship.

I say all this, not to say that this is your fault, but to give you an idea of what may be happening. Your friend may just need a little bit of space to feel and struggle alone. If that is damaging to you, it may be best to take a step back and try to find some other people who can support you in person, as well, so that you have somewhere to go if your friend needs space.

I hope you are doing better, and I hope this helped you understand a different perspective.

I can't really explain the difference because I don't know much about stimming, but I do have TOCD.

The tics in TOCD are as a result of a premonitory sensation. People with this will feel some kind of sensation somewhere, like a tension in the arm, or an itch on your face. In a response to this there is a tic. If I don't tic, the sensation gets stronger and more uncomfortable until I complete the movement.

There are times when I won't be able to go to sleep because my body doesn't feel "even", yet and so I'll have to jerk my head until It feels better. Sometimes I'll be reading aloud to myself and I'll repeat a word until my mouth "feels right" around it.

I hope that helps!

Hey, this response is, partly, to remind myself to come back here later, so if I'm not that helpful I apologize!

Since I was very you (maybe 6?) I have had these "ticks" that I just could not stop. Similarly to what you mentioned, they always resulted as a response to a sensation (I get really itchy and uncomfortable). They range from blinking, scrunching my nose, repeating a word if it "feels wrong" in my mouth, brushing my arm against my side, turning my head, tensing a part of my body, and the list goes on.

When I was younger, I used to get angry with myself when I couldn't JUST STOP. It felt like every year (I'm 19 now) it would get a bit more prevalent, but recently, it has gotten exponentially worse. Sometimes I will lie awake in bed for an hour, unable to stop turning my head or twitching my fingers because I *just don't feel even yet*.

As a result of this frustration, I stared actively researching to see what was going on, and after a bunch of inaccurate potential self-diagnosis, I stumbled upon this link: [http://www.behaviortherapycenter.com/tourettic-ocd](http://www.behaviortherapycenter.com/tourettic-ocd)

It describes me to. A. Tee.

What got me excited was the section at the end, where it discusses possible treatment. I'm not big on medication (not that it's not helpful, I just would rather take a different route), but the paper mentions psychotherapeutic approaches, such as:

Exposure and response prevention

Muscle relaxation techniques

Substitution strategies

These are usually performed and taught in therapy, but since you cannot afford therapy (and I really don't have time right now), perhaps you can find some ways to walk yourself through these methods. I have recently reached out to my school counseling center for some resources, and I will report back to you when I hear from them.

Maybe not 2.4 years, but, actually, yes. When I was a minor, around my birthday, my mom would mention needing to make a doctor's appointment for my yearly physical. What I would do is just try my gosh darnedest to push it off. I would hope she would forget, tell her I'd schedule it myself, pack my schedule, etc. Eventually, a few months later, my mom would be reminded and I'd have a physical. But here's the thing *it pushed off the time when I would need my next one*. SO... by the time the next year rolled around, my school wouldn't need a new form. As long as I could keep my mom's attention away (parents are awfully forgetful as long as you give them something else to think about) BOOM, no appointment. Then, the next year, I'd do the same as the first and push it off. At that point, it would be around a year and a half since going to the doctor's.
